key_claims: Eating less protein appears to improve metabolism, reduce inflammation and cellular damage, and activate pathways linked to healthier aging and longer life.
Protein restriction can improve metabolism, alter the way cells react to nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help cells maintain normal function.
Recent human clinical trials found that people who lowered their protein intake lost weight and body fat and showed improvements in fasting blood sugar, despite often consuming more total calories.
Lower protein intake is linked to increased levels of the hormone FGF21, which can raise energy expenditure, improve blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

Excessive intake of certain amino acids (methionine, isoleucine, valine) may activate biological pathways that encourage growth and may increase the risk of obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.
limitations: The review is based on a mix of animal and human studies, and the effects in humans may differ.
The source does not specify the exact amount of protein reduction or the duration needed for benefits.
The source notes that some groups, such as pregnant women and certain older adults, may require more protein, indicating that recommendations are not one-size-fits-all.
The source does not provide quantitative data on the magnitude of benefits or risks.
what_not_to_say: The source does not claim that eating less protein will definitely slow aging in humans.
The source does not claim that protein restriction is a substitute for calorie restriction.
The source does not claim that all sedentary people should reduce protein intake.
The source does not claim that higher protein intake is harmful for everyone.
